plain_english: I think this is what Democritus meant when he said, "Anyone who wants peace of mind shouldn't take on too much business, public or private." Of course, he was talking about unnecessary business. When duty calls, we should handle all the business we need to — even endless amounts of it, both public and private. But when no serious obligation requires us to act, we're better off staying quiet. Someone who does too many things often puts himself at the mercy of Fortune. It's safest not to test her too often. Always remember she exists, and never count on anything as guaranteed. Say instead: "I'll set sail unless something stops me. I'll become praetor if nothing gets in my way. My business deals will work out unless something goes wrong." This is why we say nothing happens to a wise person that he didn't expect. We don't make him immune to life's chances, just to life's mistakes. Everything doesn't happen as he wished, but as he thought it would. His first thought was always that his plans might hit some obstacle. Disappointed hopes hurt much less when you were never completely confident of success.
original_excerpt: It was, I imagine, following out this principle that Democritis taught that “he who would live at peace must not do much business either public or private,” referring of course to unnecessary business: for if there be any necessity for it we ought to transact not only much but endless business, both public and private; in cases, however, where no solemn duty invites us to act, we had better keep ourselves quiet: for he who does many things often puts himself in Fortune’s power, and it is safest not to tempt her often, but always to remember her existence, and never to promise oneself anything on her security. I will set sail unless anything happens to prevent me, I shall be praetor, if nothing hinders me, my financial operations will succeed, unless anything goes wrong with them. This is why we say that nothing befals the wise man which he did not expect—we do not make him exempt from the chances of human life, but from its mistakes, nor does everything happen to him as he wished it would, but as he thought it would: now his first thought was that his purpose might meet with some resistance, and the pain of disappointed wishes must affect a man’s mind less severely if he has not been at all events confident of success.
